preamble: * there is an error in the clue and solution for 12 down

clue.text: A number work very hard

definitions.meaning: a number is a tune or melody, which is one sense of the word
to labour hard or exert oneself to the limit

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a single number keeps them toiling away.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both a musical air and the act of exerting oneself to breaking point, two quite separate senses.

clue.text: See 19
Mountain meat and drink for man on top?

parts.note: an alp is a high mountain, as in the Swiss Alps
ham is cured pork, a familiar meat
ale is beer, a common drink

explanation.surface: A menu of mountain fare fit for whoever comes out on top.
explanation.definitionFit: The dominant male in a group is the leader, the one who sits at the top of the pecking order.

clue.text: Natural condition in horse that's mounted, shame non-starter

indicators.note: in a down clue something mounted is raised up, so the word for the horse reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a dun is a horse of greyish-brown colour

indicators.note: a non-starter loses its first letter, so the word for shame drops its opening

parts.note: 'what a shame' means 'what a pity'

explanation.surface: A rider on a horse feels shame about being in the buff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's mounted' turns DUN into NUD; 'non-starter' takes P from PITY, leaving ITY. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being naked is the state one is born in, so it is called the natural condition, a humorous euphemism.

clue.text: Big brains, say, Shed, Arachne and Gordius, each only beginning to appear addled

parts.note: EG, for example, means 'say'

indicators.note: addled means muddled or confused, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only the opening letter of each of the two setter names is used

explanation.surface: A remark that three crossword setters have gone soft in the head despite their cleverness.
explanation.walkthrough: Arachne and Gordius are fellow Guardian setters; their first letters A and G join EG and SHED, and 'addled' scrambles all eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Highbrow intellectuals are informally called by this name, a jokey term for brainy people.

clue.text: Old, doddering man? Protect the woman with child

parts.note: EX- means former or old, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: doddering means shaky and unsteady, so the following letters wobble into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A frail old man is urged to look after a pregnant woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who is with child is pregnant, awaiting her baby's birth, the usual phrase for a mother-to-be.

clue.text: Monstrous party on the up through Gulf War not all bad

indicators.note: the reversed party passes through the jumbled letters, sitting inside them
bad signals that the letters go wrong, being rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: not all of the word War is used: its last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means read from the bottom, so the word for party is turned round

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A grim verdict on the 1991 conflict in the Gulf, with a party somehow involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not all' drops the last letter of War; 'bad' scrambles the result with Gulf into GAWFUL; 'on the up' turns the party round, and 'through' sets it after the G.
explanation.definitionFit: Something appalling or dreadful is informally called godawful, so monstrous serves as a synonym.

clue.text: The King, last of the Georges, detailed other guards

indicators.note: the shortened word for other surrounds, or guards, the regnal number
de-tailed means having the tail cut off, so the final letter goes

parts.note: else means other, as in 'someone else'
George VI was the last British king named George

explanation.surface: A claim that the final King George was protected by others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' cuts off the last letter, and 'guards' wraps what is left round the Roman numeral. Elvis Presley was nicknamed the King of rock and roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvis Presley was known as the King of Rock and Roll, so the title identifies him.

clue.text: Office with something to do overly upset to discover wheel clamp

parts.note: a den is a study or private room for working, an office
a verb is a doing word, a word for an action

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word for overly reads upwards

parts.note: too means excessively, overly

explanation.surface: An office worker, with too much to do, is upset to find their car clamped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns TOO into OOT. 'to discover' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Denver boot is the American name for a device locked on a car wheel to immobilise it.

clue.text: Uncle Sam's duck and young dog biting Miliband, held by teeth

parts.note: a duck is zero in cricket, and Americans say zip for zero

indicators.note: the young dog bites into the name, holding it inside its mouth

parts.note: a pup is a young dog
Ed Miliband was leader of the UK Labour Party

explanation.surface: An American duck and a puppy chew on a politician.
explanation.definitionFit: A fastened zip is closed by its interlocking teeth, so a garment held shut by teeth is zipped up.

clue.text: Sport that's practised by cheating footballers

definitions.meaning: an Olympic sport of plunging into water from a board
throwing oneself to the ground to win a foul unfairly in football

explanation.surface: A dig at footballers who fall over to cheat their way to a free kick.
explanation.definitionFit: The aquatic sport of jumping from a board, and footballers' feigned falls to win fouls, share one word.

clue.text: Montezuma's revenge, as three times we cope, desperate to contain unknown quantity

indicators.note: the scrambled letters hold the algebraic unknown inside them
desperate suggests wild and frantic, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time, and three times gives three of them
the second of the three Ts for times
the third of the three Ts for times
taken as written
taken as written
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknowns, here z

explanation.surface: A traveller struck by stomach trouble struggles, again and again, to cope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to contain' puts Z inside the letters 'desperate' scrambles. Montezuma's revenge is slang for traveller's diarrhoea, and so is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are humorous slang for the diarrhoea that visitors to Mexico suffer, named after Aztec ruler Montezuma.

clue.text: With marathon over, cruciate damage ends in the knife

indicators.note: in a down clue over means above, so the chocolate bar comes first

parts.note: Marathon was the old British name of the Snickers chocolate bar

indicators.note: only the final letter of each of the two words is taken

explanation.surface: After running a marathon, a damaged knee ligament ends up under the surgeon's knife.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble admits an error: the real knife is SNICKERSNEE, but the wordplay as printed builds this ten-letter form. 'in the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A snickersnee is an old word for a large knife used for fighting, which the grid entry stands for.

clue.text: Ancient vessel avoiding the banks

indicators.note: the banks are the two edges, which are left off the word for vessel

parts.note: a tin can is a metal container, a vessel

explanation.surface: An old ship steers clear of the riverbanks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient' is a noun here: a person of an old civilisation. 'vessel' looks like a ship, but it is a tin can.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the old South American empire of Peru is one of the ancients, a person from antiquity.

clue.text: An addiction to lager, might one say, not entirely capital?

parts.note: an gives the article A
Bud, short for Budweiser, is a brand of lager

indicators.note: the word for addiction is not complete: its last letter is cut

parts.note: a habit is an addiction

explanation.surface: A drinker is asked whether their beer habit has become a capital offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' cuts HABIT to HABI. 'might one say' and 'to' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Abu Dhabi is the capital city of the United Arab Emirates.

clue.text: Swiss city seen during break, abandoning American and English winter

indicators.note: the Swiss city is seen in the middle of the other letters
the word for break leaves behind the letters for American

parts.note: a hiatus is a break or pause
US stands for United States, so American
Bern is the capital of Switzerland

explanation.surface: A traveller breaks a trip in Switzerland, leaving the Americans and English to spend the winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoning' strips the American letters from the break, leaving HIAT, then E is added; 'seen during' sets the Swiss capital inside. 'winter' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that hibernate pass the cold season dormant, so to winter, as a verb, is a synonym.

clue.text: Bully runs from hunter, travelling north always

indicators.note: in a down clue going north is going upwards, so the letters read backwards
runs is taken away from the word for hunter

parts.note: Nimrod was the mighty hunter of the Bible
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
e'er is a poetic contraction of ever, always

explanation.surface: A bully flees from a hunter, forever heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' removes R from NIMROD, leaving NIMOD, and 'travelling north' turns it into DOMIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To bully someone is to lord it over them, which is what domineering means, so the verbs match.

clue.text: Demonstrated as cadet suggested?

parts.note: read cryptically, ACTED with OUT as an instruction to scramble it yields the clue word cadet

explanation.surface: A young recruit performed exactly as he had proposed.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: ACTED OUT, read as wordplay, means 'ACTED, rearranged', and the letters of ACTED rearranged are CADET.
explanation.definitionFit: To act something out is to perform or demonstrate it physically, as in a game of charades.

clue.text: Reserve suggesting no need for deodorant?

definitions.meaning: to ... a table or seat is to reserve it
body odour is fine, so no deodorant is needed

explanation.surface: A notice about a reservation hints that nobody needs to worry about smelling.
explanation.walkthrough: BO is short for body odour, so the answer split in two says body odour is OK.
explanation.definitionFit: To book is to reserve a place, ticket or table in advance.

clue.text: Die in ghetto with whip-round

indicators.note: round suggests turning the letters about, a rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone dies in a ghetto, and a collection is taken for the funeral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whip-round' looks like one word, a collection; 'round' is the anagram signal. 'in' and 'with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop the twig is old British slang for dying, like kick the bucket.

clue.text: Kaleidoscopic expression coming up now certainly — ouch, that's horrible!

indicators.note: something horrible is messed up, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A colourful remark is made with certainty, followed by a cry of pain at something nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's' is a link. The answer is slang for vomiting, the colourful thing that comes up.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for vomit: a many-coloured gape of the mouth as food comes back up, hence a kaleidoscopic expression.

clue.text: Lifting mechanism that's stolen, is nicked

indicators.note: the word for stolen nicks, or takes in, the little word is

parts.note: hot is slang for stolen goods
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crane that is stolen property has been nicked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nicked' is British slang for stolen; here it signals HOT capturing IS. 'that's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoist is a device for raising heavy loads, such as a pulley or winch.

clue.text: See 20
Plan with fury to go after poisoner

indicators.note: the word for fury is placed after the word for poisoner

parts.note: an asp is a venomous snake, which kills with poison
ire is anger or fury

explanation.surface: A scheme is hatched to chase a poisoner in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to aim at or set one's sights on something, which is a sense of planning or intending.

clue.text: Will lover melt heart of snake in the grass?

indicators.note: the melting and the snake's heart go inside the grass

parts.note: hay is dried grass
to thaw is to melt

indicators.note: the middle letter of the word snake is taken

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a lover will soften the heart of a treacherous snake in the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' is Shakespeare, whose wife was Anne Hathaway. 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Hathaway married William Shakespeare, so she was the bard's lover and wife.

clue.text: Don having loose skin, temperature picked up by doctor?

indicators.note: the skin of a word is its outside, its first and last letters
the doctor picks up the temperature, taking it in among their letters

parts.note: a curer is one who cures, a doctor

explanation.surface: A university teacher with sagging skin has their temperature taken by a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' is a university teacher, not the verb meaning put on. 'having' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A don is a teacher at Oxford or Cambridge, and such a teacher gives lectures to students.

clue.text: River boat not launching, they all leave the stage

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, England

indicators.note: not launching means the boat loses its start, the first letter

parts.note: a punt is a flat-bottomed river boat

explanation.surface: A boat fails to launch on the river, and the actors all walk off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not launching' trims PUNT to UNT. Exeunt is the Latin stage direction meaning they go out.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeunt is the stage direction in a play script that tells several actors to go off.
